344.title: Babel (Genesis 11:1–9)
344.hook: a tower to make a name for ourselves, and the scattering
344.howItsDone: The Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9) is one of the readings offered at the Vigil Mass of Pentecost, where the Church sets it beside the gift of tongues in Acts 2.

segments.voice: Yesterday, covenant: a bow in the clouds and a promise to every creature. What small promise did you keep to a living thing? A new week starts. Day three hundred forty-four.

A new tower goes up downtown, and somebody's name goes on the top in steel letters, lit up at night. A few years later, someone else builds higher. Genesis tells its own tower story in nine verses. After the flood, the whole earth has one language and one way of speaking. People move and settle on a plain in the land of Sennaar. And someone has a new idea. Not stone. Bricks, baked hard in a fire, with tar for mortar. A new technology. And with it, a plan.
screen: `A NAME IN STEEL LETTERS.` → `ONE LANGUAGE, ONE PLAIN.` → `BAKED BRICKS AND A PLAN.`

segments.voice: First, the plan, in the Douay-Rheims. They say: come, let us make a city and a tower, the top of which may reach to heaven, "and let us make our name famous before we be scattered abroad into all lands." Notice what they want. Not God's name. Their own. And notice the fear underneath: before we be scattered. A tower to hold everyone in one place, under one name. Second, the irony. The tower is meant to reach heaven, but the text says God comes down to see it. However tall, it's so small that God has to come down to look. Third, the scattering. God confuses their language so they can't understand one another, and they stop building and spread across the earth: exactly what they were afraid of. The city is called Babel. In Hebrew it sounds like balal, to confuse or mix up. It's also the Hebrew name for Babylon. Fourth, how the Church reads it. Babel isn't only a punishment. The Catechism reads the spreading of the nations as part of God's plan after the flood, a world of many peoples. And some Christian readers, Church Fathers among them, read Pentecost as Babel turned inside out. At Babel, one language breaks into many and nobody understands. At Pentecost, the apostles speak, and people from many nations each hear them in their own language. The Church even offers the Babel story as a reading at the Vigil of Pentecost. Not one name over everyone. Many voices, understood.
screen: `LET US MAKE OUR NAME FAMOUS.` · `GOD COMES DOWN TO SEE IT.` · `BABEL, BALAL: CONFUSED.` · `PENTECOST, BABEL INSIDE OUT.` · then, large: `NOT OUR NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do something without needing credit. Settle, and breathe. Think through the next day. Where could you do a good thing that nobody will trace back to you? Refill the coffee no one refills. Fix a typo in a shared document. Leave a kind review without your name. Pay a small compliment about someone to a third person, and not to them. Choose one. Notice the small itch to be seen doing it, and let it go. If you pray, you can offer it for God's name, not yours. The bell holds the time.
Babel. The city of the tower, built to make a name. In Hebrew it sounds like the word for confusion, and it's the same name as Babylon.
Your line: not our name. Today, do your one uncredited good thing, and don't mention it to anyone, even later. Day three hundred forty-four.

345.title: Go forth (Genesis 12:1–9)
345.hook: Abram, seventy-five, leaves his country for a land God will show him
345.carry: go, and I will show you
345.howItsDone: Catholics call Abraham their father in faith; he is named in the Roman Canon at Mass, and the call of Abram (Genesis 12:1–4) is read on the Second Sunday of Lent in one year of the cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Babel: a tower to make a name, and a scattering. Your line was not our name. Did you manage one good thing with no credit? Today, God promises a name to one man. Day three hundred forty-five.

Seventy-five can be an age for settling in: the house paid off, or close, a pharmacist who knows your name. Abram, at seventy-five, packs everything onto animals, says goodbye to the town where his father died, and heads out with no address. Not a retirement village. Not a place he's seen in photos. Just a direction, and a voice that said go. After eleven chapters about the whole world, Genesis zooms in on one old man and his first step.
screen: `SEVENTY-FIVE, AN AGE FOR SETTLING.` → `PACKING WITH NO ADDRESS.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD, THEN ONE MAN.`

segments.voice: First, the call. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the Lord said to Abram: Go forth out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and out of thy father's house, and come into the land which I shall shew thee." Three circles to leave, each one closer than the last: country, kindred, father's house. And one thing in exchange: a land God hasn't named yet. Which I shall show thee. The map comes after the step. In Hebrew, go forth is lekh lekha, and some Jewish teachers hear it as go to yourself, as if leaving home were also a way of becoming who you are. Second, the promise. I will make of thee a great nation, God says, and make thy name great. Notice the echo. At Babel, people tried to make a name for themselves. Here, God gives one. And then the widest line: in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Not just Abram's family. Everyone. Third, the response. Genesis doesn't record a word from Abram. It just says he went, as the Lord had told him. He was seventy-five. He took Sarai, his nephew Lot, and everything they had, and walked to Canaan, and built altars along the way. Fourth, how the Church remembers him. The Letter to the Hebrews says Abraham went out not knowing where he was going. The Catechism calls him the father of all who believe, and at Mass, the first Eucharistic Prayer names him our father in faith. The Catechism holds him up as a model of faith: not knowing the whole map, but taking the first step.
screen: `COUNTRY, KINDRED, FATHER'S HOUSE.` · `THE MAP COMES AFTER THE STEP.` · `GOD GIVES THE NAME.` · `ABRAM WENT, AT SEVENTY-FIVE.` · then, large: `GO FORTH OUT OF THY COUNTRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step without the full map. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that's waiting on you to have it all figured out first: a conversation, a change, an application, a call you keep not making. Notice how much of the map you want before you'll move. Now ask a smaller question: what's the first step, just the first? Picture yourself taking it. Not the whole road. One step. If you pray, you can ask God to show the next part when it's time. The bell holds the time.
Go forth. Lekh lekha in Hebrew: God's call to Abram to leave his country for a land not yet shown. He went, at seventy-five.
Your line: go, and I will show you. Today, take the first step you pictured, before you feel ready, and let the next one wait. Day three hundred forty-five.

346.title: Bread and wine (Genesis 14:17–20)
346.hook: Melchisedech, king and priest, brings out bread and wine; named in the Roman Canon
346.howItsDone: In the Roman Canon, the priest asks God to accept the Mass's offering as he accepted the offering of Melchisedech, and Genesis 14:18–20 is read on the solemnity of the Body and Blood of Christ in one year of the cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, go forth: Abram at seventy-five, walking with no map. Your line was go, and I will show you. What first step did you take? Day three hundred forty-six.

Some characters in the Bible get whole books. Some get a chapter. This one gets three verses, and then vanishes. Abram has just come back from a night raid. Four kings had carried off his nephew Lot, and Abram chased them north with three hundred eighteen men and brought everyone home. He's tired, dusty, a winner. On the road back, a king comes out to meet him. Not with an army. Not with a bill. With bread, and wine. And then he's gone from the story, and yet his name is still spoken in a prayer at Catholic altars.
screen: `A NIGHT RAID, LOT RESCUED.` → `A KING COMES OUT TO MEET HIM.` → `THREE VERSES, THEN GONE.`

segments.voice: First, who he is. In the Douay-Rheims: "But Melchisedech the king of Salem, bringing forth bread and wine, for he was the priest of the most high God." A king and a priest at once. His name in Hebrew means king of righteousness. Salem means peace, and later tradition identifies it with Jerusalem. He has no family tree, no beginning or end in the story. He just appears. Second, what he does. He blesses Abram by the most high God, maker of heaven and earth, and he blesses God for the victory. And Abram gives him a tenth of everything. The man God called to be a blessing is himself blessed by a stranger. Third, where he turns up again. In a psalm, God says to the king, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech." And the Letter to the Hebrews takes that line and applies it to Christ: a priest not by birth in Aaron's family, but like Melchisedech, forever. Fourth, why Catholics say his name. In the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass, the priest asks God to accept the offering as he once accepted the gifts of Abel, the sacrifice of Abraham, and the offering of the high priest Melchisedech. The Catechism sees in his bread and wine a sign that points ahead to the Eucharist. Readers in other churches, following Hebrews, also see in him a picture of Christ's priesthood, and draw the link to the altar differently or not at all. Either way, the shape is the same: a priest, a blessing, bread and wine, long ago.
screen: `A KING AND A PRIEST AT ONCE.` · `ABRAM IS BLESSED AND GIVES A TENTH.` · `A PRIEST FOREVER, IN THE PSALM.` · `NAMED IN THE ROMAN CANON.` · then, large: `BRINGING FORTH BREAD AND WINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice bread and wine as signs. If there's bread, or a cracker, or any food nearby, put it in front of you. If not, picture a loaf on a table. Settle, and breathe. Think about how much it took to get here: wheat in a field, rain, someone's hands at harvest, an oven, a truck. Grapes on a vine, crushed and waited on. Ordinary things that took a long time and many people. Let that sink in. If you pray, you can give thanks for the food in front of you and for the people who brought it to you. The bell holds the time.
Melchisedech, the king and priest who brought out bread and wine to bless Abram, a sign Catholics see of the Eucharist. Today's word.
Your line: bread and wine, long ago. Today, at one meal, take the first bite slowly and remember how far it came to reach you. Day three hundred forty-six.

347.title: Count the stars (Genesis 15:1–6)
347.hook: a childless old man is told to count the stars, and believes
347.howItsDone: Catholics call Abraham their father in faith, and Genesis 15:5–6 is read with Paul's letters in the liturgy; the Catechism presents Abraham as the model of the obedience of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bread and wine, Melchisedech: a priest-king on the road, and a blessing. Your line was bread and wine, long ago. Which bite did you take slowly? Day three hundred forty-seven.

Abram has land promised, a great name promised, a nation promised. What he doesn't have is a single child. Years have gone by since he left home. He's won a war and been blessed by a king, and still the tent is quiet. So when God speaks to him in a vision and says fear not, I am thy reward, Abram finally says the hard thing out loud. What will you give me? I'm going childless, and a servant in my house, Eliezer of Damascus, is going to inherit everything. It's the first time in the story Abram argues back. And God's answer is to take him outside.
screen: `EVERYTHING PROMISED BUT A CHILD.` → `WHAT WILL YOU GIVE ME?` → `GOD TAKES HIM OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the sky. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he brought him forth abroad, and said to him: Look up to heaven and number the stars, if thou canst. And he said to him: So shall thy seed be." Picture it with no city lights at all. Thousands of stars, the river of the Milky Way. God doesn't answer the complaint with an argument. God gives Abram something to look at. Count them, if you can. Second, the response, one short verse: "Abram believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice." Reputed means counted, credited. Unto justice means as righteousness. The Hebrew verb for believed comes from the same root as amen: to be firm, to lean your weight on something. Abram leans his weight on the promise. Nothing has changed yet. He's still old, Sarai's still childless, the tent's still quiet. He believes anyway. Third, the line's long life. Saint Paul quotes it in his letters to the Romans and the Galatians: Abraham believed, and it was counted to him. The Letter of James quotes it too, and sets it beside Abraham's deeds. Catholics read Paul and James together: a faith that is alive, and shows itself in love. Many Protestant churches put the emphasis on faith alone. In 1999, Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration saying they share a basic understanding of this, while still differing on some points. Fourth, the stars themselves. The Letter to the Hebrews looks back on this night: from one man, and him as good as dead, came children as many as the stars of heaven. Paul calls Abraham the father of all who believe, which is why Catholics speak of him as our father in faith. Jews and Muslims call him father too. A man who couldn't see one grandchild was asked to look up anyway.
screen: `NUMBER THE STARS, IF THOU CANST.` · `ABRAM BELIEVED GOD.` · `THE SAME ROOT AS AMEN.` · `PAUL AND JAMES BOTH QUOTE IT.` · then, large: `SO SHALL THY SEED BE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the night sky. If it's night where you are, step outside or go to a window. If it's daytime, close your eyes and remember the clearest night sky you've ever seen. Settle, and breathe. Start counting, slowly. One. Two. Three. Don't rush. Somewhere past ten you'll lose your place. Let yourself lose it. Notice how big the sky is and how small the counting is. If you pray, you can name a promise you're still waiting on, and leave it up there. The bell holds the time.
Amen, the root behind Abram believed: to be firm, to lean your weight on a promise before anything has changed. Today's word.
Your line: so shall thy seed be. Tonight, look up for one minute before bed, even through a window, and remember someone who's still waiting on something. Day three hundred forty-seven.

348.title: The God who sees (Genesis 16)
348.hook: Hagar, a runaway slave, gives God a name
348.howItsDone: Catholic social teaching speaks of God hearing the cry of the poor and of a special care for those pushed to the margins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, count the stars, amen: an old man told to look up, and he believed. Your line was so shall thy seed be. Did you look up last night? Today, someone in the same household nobody looks at. Day three hundred forty-eight.

Abram and Sarai have lived ten years in Canaan, still with no child, and Sarai has stopped waiting. She takes matters into her own hands: she gives her Egyptian slave, a young woman named Hagar, to Abram, so a child can be born on her behalf. Hagar conceives. And the household cracks. Hagar looks down on Sarai; Sarai treats her harshly; Abram says, she's your slave, do what you like. So Hagar runs. Pregnant, alone, into the desert, on the road toward Egypt. Nobody comes after her. Nobody in the camp, anyway.
screen: `A SLAVE GIVEN TO ABRAM.` → `THE HOUSEHOLD CRACKS.` → `HAGAR RUNS INTO THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: First, the finding. By a spring of water in the wilderness, on the road to Shur, the angel of the Lord finds her. And notice the first thing said to her. In the Douay-Rheims: "Agar, handmaid of Sarai, whence comest thou? and whither goest thou?" Agar is the old spelling of Hagar. Two things here. The angel calls her by name. In this chapter, Abram and Sarai never once say her name; she's my handmaid, your handmaid. And the angel asks her questions, as if her answer matters. Second, the hard part. The angel tells her to go back and submit to Sarai. The text doesn't soften that, and we shouldn't either. But with it comes a promise: her descendants will be too many to count, and her son will be named Ishmael, which means God hears, because the Lord has heard her affliction. Third, the name. And then Hagar does something remarkable: she gives God a name. In the Douay-Rheims: "Thou the God who hast seen me." In Hebrew, El Roi, the God who sees. Not Abram. Not a priest. An Egyptian slave woman, pregnant, on the run, by a well in the desert. The well itself is named after it. Fourth, why it lasts. Catholic social teaching speaks of a God who hears the cry of the poor and sees the overlooked. Readers find that God here, by a spring in the desert. The person with the least power in the camp is the one who says who God is to her.
screen: `FOUND BY A SPRING, CALLED BY NAME.` · `GO BACK: THE TEXT DOESN'T SOFTEN IT.` · `ISHMAEL: GOD HEARS.` · `EL ROI: SHE NAMES GOD.` · then, large: `THOU THE GOD WHO HAST SEEN ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice someone overlooked. Settle, and breathe. Think back through yesterday. Who was there that you didn't really see? The cashier. The cleaner leaving the office as you arrived. The kid at the edge of the playground. The relative who never gets asked a question at dinner. Pick one. Say their name to yourself, if you know it. If you don't, notice that. Picture their face as clearly as you can. If you pray, you can hold them before the God who sees. The bell holds the time.
El Roi, the God who sees: the name Hagar, a runaway slave in the desert, gives to God by a spring. Today's word.
Your line: thou god who seest me. Today, learn the name of one person you see often but have never really looked at, and use it. Day three hundred forty-eight.

349.title: Three visitors at Mamre (Genesis 18:1–15)
349.hook: Abraham runs to feed three strangers; Christians painted them as the Trinity
349.howItsDone: Benedictine monasteries still follow Saint Benedict's rule to receive every guest as Christ, and Rublev's icon of the three visitors, often called the Trinity, is used for prayer by Catholics and Orthodox Christians alike.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the God who sees, El Roi: Hagar by a desert spring, naming God. Your line was thou god who seest me. Whose name did you learn? Day three hundred forty-nine.

A Russian icon, painted by a monk, is copied onto cards and walls in churches and homes far from Russia. Three figures with wings sit around a table. Their heads tilt toward one another. In the middle of the table there's a cup. The fourth side of the table, the side facing you, is empty, as if there's a place left open. The painter, a monk named Andrei Rublev, didn't invent the scene. The icon is known as the Trinity, but what it shows is a moment from Genesis: an old man's lunch with three strangers who showed up at noon.
screen: `THREE FIGURES AROUND A TABLE.` → `THE FOURTH SIDE IS OPEN.` → `A LUNCH FROM GENESIS.`

segments.voice: First, the scene. Abraham is sitting at the door of his tent by the oaks of Mamre, in the Douay-Rheims, "in the very heat of the day." The worst hour to have guests. He looks up and sees three men standing nearby. And the old man doesn't wait. Genesis says "he ran to meet them from the door of his tent" and bowed to the ground. Second, the feast. He offers a little water and a morsel of bread, and then makes it much more. He hurries to Sarah: three measures of fine flour, make cakes. He runs to the herd for a tender calf. He brings butter and milk, and stands by them under the tree while they eat. A morsel turns into a banquet. Third, who they are. The text keeps shifting. Three men. Then the Lord speaks. Then two of them go on toward Sodom as angels. Genesis never explains it. Jewish tradition reads the three as angels sent by God. Some Christian writers, Ambrose and Augustine among them, saw a hint of the Trinity, which is what Rublev painted. And one visitor makes a promise: by this time next year, Sarah will have a son. Behind the tent door, Sarah laughs. Fourth, what the Church took from it. The Letter to the Hebrews says not to forget hospitality, because some, by it, have entertained angels without knowing. Saint Benedict told his monks to welcome every guest as Christ himself. In Greek, hospitality is philoxenia: love of the stranger.
screen: `THE DOOR OF THE TENT, AT NOON.` · `A MORSEL BECOMES A FEAST.` · `THREE MEN, THE LORD, OR ANGELS?` · `WELCOME EVERY GUEST AS CHRIST.` · then, large: `HE RAN TO MEET THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer a guest something good. Settle, and breathe. Picture the next person likely to come through your door, or sit at your desk, or join your table. A friend, a delivery driver, a coworker, a child's friend after school. Now picture Abraham, running in the heat. What could you offer them that's a little more than a morsel? A real drink. A chair. Your full attention for five minutes. Something from the good shelf. Choose it now. If you pray, you can ask to see Christ in whoever comes. The bell holds the time.
Hospitality. Philoxenia in Greek, love of the stranger. Abraham running at noon to feed three visitors who turn out to carry God's promise.
Your line: strangers bring god. Today, when someone unexpected interrupts you, treat the interruption like a visitor at the tent door. Day three hundred forty-nine.

what a scholar hears: the visitors shift between three men, the Lord and angels; Augustine and others saw the Trinity, and Rublev painted it.

350.title: Abraham bargains (Genesis 18:16–33)
350.hook: fifty righteous, forty, thirty, ten: Abraham argues with God for a city
350.howItsDone: At Mass, the prayer of the faithful asks God's help for the Church, the world, people in need and the local community, and Catholics also pray for others by name in their own prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hospitality: an old man running at noon to feed three strangers. Your line was strangers bring god. Who interrupted you, and how did you welcome them? Day three hundred fifty, the end of the week.

At a yard sale, haggling has its own steps. One person names a price. The other laughs and names a lower one. Somebody walks away. Somebody calls them back. Somewhere in the middle, a deal. Genesis puts that dance somewhere no one would expect. The visitors from yesterday's lunch get up and look toward Sodom, a city the story says is full of wickedness. Abraham walks with them to see them off. And the Lord says, in effect, shall I hide from Abraham what I'm about to do? And Abraham, who just served lunch, starts to haggle with God.
screen: `THE STEPS OF A HAGGLE.` → `THE VISITORS LOOK TOWARD SODOM.` → `ABRAHAM HAGGLES WITH GOD.`

segments.voice: First, the opening bid. Abraham steps closer and asks: will you destroy the just with the wicked? Suppose there are fifty just people in the city. Will you spare it for them? And then a line that's almost shocking: shall not the judge of all the earth do what is just? He holds God to God's own justice. And God agrees: for fifty, I'll spare the whole place. Second, the haggling. Abraham keeps going, and he knows exactly how bold he's being. In the Douay-Rheims: "I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes." Dust, like the clay of the first human. And still he speaks. Forty-five? Yes. Forty? Yes. Thirty? Yes. Twenty? Yes. Again and again he humbles himself, and asks again. Third, the last number. Let not my Lord be angry, he says, I'll speak only once more. Ten? And God says: "I will not destroy it for the sake of ten." Notice who never says no. God never refuses. It's Abraham who stops asking. Fourth, how the Church reads it. The Catechism turns to this scene when it teaches about intercession, prayer on behalf of others: a friend of God standing between a city and its judgment. Catholics pray for others in the same spirit, and at Mass in the prayer of the faithful. And it closes a week that started with a tower to heaven, then a call to go forth, Melchisedech, a sky full of stars, El Roi, three visitors at a table, and now an old man bargaining for mercy.
screen: `WILL YOU DESTROY THE JUST?` · `I AM DUST AND ASHES.` · `FIFTY, FORTY, THIRTY, TWENTY, TEN.` · `GOD NEVER SAYS NO.` · then, large: `FOR THE SAKE OF TEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray boldly for a place, or if you don't pray, hold one in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Choose a place that needs mercy: your street, a hospital ward, a city in the news, a prison, a country at war. Picture it as clearly as you can, and picture the good people in it, the ones trying, even if there aren't many. If you pray, you can ask for mercy for it, and then ask again, a little more boldly, the way Abraham did. If you don't, simply wish it well, and keep wishing. The bell holds the time.
Abraham bargains. Fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten: an old man asking God, again and again, to spare a city for the sake of the just in it.
Your line: argue for mercy. Today, when someone is being written off, at work, online or at home, be the one who says: but what about the good in them? Day three hundred fifty.
